title: Regularisation: Dropout, Weight Decay and Early Stopping

thumbnail.headline: Stop Memorising, Start Generalising
thumbnail.image: Navy background, a network diagram with a few nodes greyed out, a small shield icon and a stop sign shape, headline in teal Inter Bold.

slide.title: Stop Memorising, Start Generalising
slide.body: Three icons in a row: a network with some nodes switched off (dropout), a shrinking weight (weight decay), a pause button on a loss curve (early stopping). Small tag: Deep Learning and Neural Networks · Lesson 9.

production_notes: Review flags: none. Hyperparameter ranges (dropout 0.1 to 0.5, weight decay about 1e-4 to 1e-2) are starting points for tuning, not claims about results.
The comparison result is said as 'you should see something like' (content.md: expected result). Show the real curves from the two runs; do not add numbers in captions.
train_one_epoch and evaluate are the learner's own helpers from L05; define them in a hidden cell above the demo cell before recording.
Hamid and the Agadir argan-oil cooperative are hypothetical; stock footage must not show a real company name or logo.

Hook.voiceover: In the last lesson, the validation loss started to rise while the training loss kept falling. The model was learning the training set too well. Today, you add three tools that make it learn the pattern, not the details.
Hook.on_screen_text: Learn the pattern, not the details

Explain.voiceover: Regularisation is any change that helps a model do better on new data, usually at some cost to its training score. In the scikit-learn course, you met penalties for linear models. Deep networks use the same idea, plus a few of their own.

slide.title: Regularisation
slide.body: Better on new data, at some cost to the training score. Three tools: dropout · weight decay · early stopping

Explain.voiceover: Dropout randomly switches off a fraction of the units in each training step, and scales up the rest. The network cannot rely on any single unit, so it learns features that are more spread out and more robust. It is active only in train mode. In eval mode, it does nothing. Typical rates are between ten and fifty percent.

slide.title: Dropout
slide.body: Two copies of one network: training step with random nodes greyed out; evaluation with all nodes on. Code: nn.Dropout(p), p = 0.1 to 0.5, usually before fully connected layers.

Explain.voiceover: Weight decay shrinks every weight a little at each step. This keeps the weights small and the function smoother. It is the deep-learning version of an L2 penalty. With Adam, use the AdamW optimiser, which applies the decay separately.

slide.title: Weight decay
slide.body:
opt = torch.optim.AdamW(params, lr=1e-3, weight_decay=1e-2)
# starting values about 1e-4 to 1e-2; tune on validation data

Explain.voiceover: Early stopping watches the validation loss after every epoch. It saves a copy of the weights whenever the loss improves, and stops when there has been no improvement for a set number of epochs, called the patience. Then you reload the best copy. It also saves GPU time. And remember, augmentation is a regulariser too, often the strongest one for images.

slide.title: Early stopping
slide.body: Validation loss curve: a green dot at the lowest point labelled 'save best', then 3 epochs with no improvement → 'stop' → reload best. Note: augmentation (L06) also regularises.

Explain.voiceover: Think of a student who practises with one set of past exam questions. They can memorise the answers and still fail a new exam. A student who practises with different questions, sometimes with parts hidden, must learn the method.
Explain.stock_query: student studying different practice papers at desk
Explain.on_screen_text: Practise the method, not the answers

Explain.voiceover: Dropout hides parts of the question. Weight decay stops the student from building very complicated rules. And early stopping is the teacher saying, stop now, you are starting to memorise.

slide.title: The student analogy
slide.body: Dropout = hide parts of the question · Weight decay = no over-complicated rules · Early stopping = 'stop now, you are starting to memorise'

Demonstrate.voiceover: Hamid is an engineer at an argan-oil cooperative in Agadir, Morocco. His quality-check CNN overfits after a few epochs. Let's add all three tools in Colab.
Demonstrate.stock_query: argan nuts and oil bottles on table

Demonstrate.voiceover: First, he adds a dropout layer with a rate of zero point three, just before the final linear layer. Then he switches the optimiser to AdamW, with a weight decay of zero point zero one.
screen_steps: Run the model cell from content.md: the L07 CNN with nn.Flatten(), nn.Dropout(0.3), nn.Linear(64 * 7 * 7, 10)

Demonstrate.voiceover: Next, the early-stopping block around his loop from lesson five, with a patience of three. After each epoch, if the validation loss improves, he saves a deep copy of the weights. If not, he counts a bad epoch, and after three in a row, he stops.
screen_steps: Run the early-stopping loop from content.md: best_loss, best_state, patience, bad_epochs = float("inf"), None, 3, 0; for epoch in range(30): train_one_epoch(model, opt); val_loss = evaluate(model)
Show the printed line: stopping at epoch …

Demonstrate.voiceover: At the end, he loads the best weights back into the model. Then he runs two experiments with the same data, seed and learning rate. The original model, and the regularised one.
screen_steps: Run the original model and the regularised model with the same data, seed and lr

Demonstrate.voiceover: He plots both validation curves on one chart. You should see something like this. The regularised model's validation loss stays lower for longer, and the gap between training and validation gets smaller. He compares the best scores, not the final ones, and records both runs in a small table.
screen_steps: Plot both validation loss curves on one chart with plot_curves from L08 (expected output: regularised curve lower for longer, smaller train–validation gap)
Add a two-row results table: run, best validation loss, best epoch
Demonstrate.on_screen_text: Compare best scores, not final ones

Demonstrate.voiceover: A common mistake is saving the best model without a real copy. That only stores links to the live weights, which keep changing. At the end, best is simply the last model. Use a deep copy, or save to a file. And add regularisers one at a time, or you cannot tell which one helped.
Demonstrate.on_screen_text: Save a real copy of the weights

Recap.voiceover: Let's recap. First, dropout switches off random units during training only, and weight decay keeps weights small. Both reduce overfitting, at some cost to the training fit. Second, early stopping keeps the checkpoint with the best validation loss, and stops after a set number of epochs without improvement. Third, judge each regulariser by comparing validation curves across runs that change one thing at a time.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Dropout (training only) and weight decay reduce overfitting. 2. Early stopping keeps the best checkpoint; deep-copy the weights. 3. Compare validation curves, one change at a time.

CTA.voiceover: Now it is your turn. In the exercise below this video, you will add dropout and weight decay to your own CNN, use early stopping, and compare the validation curves before and after. It takes about forty minutes. In the next lesson, we save a lot of training time with transfer learning and pretrained CNNs. See you there.
